questions.q: Name the ceremony that formally created the bond between a lord and a vassal in medieval Europe, and state the two key acts performed during it.
questions.a: The ceremony was called *homage and fealty*. The vassal knelt, placed his hands between the lord's (homage), and swore an oath of loyalty on a relic or the Gospels (fealty). A wrong answer—such as naming "investiture" (which is the grant of the fief, not the personal bond) or confusing it with a coronation—reveals the student conflates the legal grant of land with the personal act of submission that defined feudalism.

questions.q: Why did primogeniture (inheritance by the eldest son) become the dominant inheritance custom among the European nobility by the 12th century?
questions.a: Primogeniture prevented the fragmentation of fiefs, which would weaken the military capacity of the vassal and undermine the lord's ability to summon a coherent force; it also concentrated wealth and status, reinforcing the nobility's cohesion as a ruling class. A wrong answer focusing only on "keeping the family rich" misses the structural feudal logic: a divided fief meant a divided quota of knights, threatening the entire lord-vassal pyramid.

questions.q: A 12th-century charter records that a knight holds a fief of 500 hectares and owes 40 days of military service annually. If the king calls for a 90-day campaign, explain how the knight's obligation is typically fulfilled and what this reveals about the limits of feudal levies.
questions.a: The knight serves 40 days at his own cost; beyond that, the lord must pay wages (scutage) or the knight may refuse. This shows feudal levies were short-term and financially bounded, forcing monarchs to develop paid armies (mercenaries) for sustained wars—a key reason feudalism declined. A wrong answer claiming the knight serves 90 days unconditionally ignores the contractual, limited nature of feudal service.

questions.q: Compare the European knight's code of chivalry with the Rajput concept of *maryada* (honour). Identify two similarities and one fundamental difference in how each code regulated violence.
questions.a: Similarities: both idealised protection of the weak, loyalty to one's lord/clan, and ritualised combat (tournaments vs. *yudh*). Difference: chivalry was a trans-national, Church-influenced code that attempted to Christianise warfare (e.g., Peace of God, Truce of God), whereas *maryada* was clan-based and tied to *dharma* without a universal ecclesiastical authority. A wrong answer treating them as identical overlooks the Church's role in shaping chivalry—a uniquely European feature.

questions.q: Evaluate the claim: "The nobility's monopoly on warfare disappeared because gunpowder made castles and armour obsolete." Provide two pieces of evidence that support and two that challenge this view.
questions.a: Support: (1) cannon breached curtain walls (e.g., Constantinople 1453), reducing castle value; (2) arquebuses pierced plate armour, diminishing the knight's battlefield dominance. Challenge: (1) nobles adapted by becoming officers in standing armies, retaining social prestige; (2) many nobles owned the new artillery and gunpowder works, profiting from the technology. A one-sided answer reveals an inability to see social groups as adaptive, not just passive victims of technology.

questions.q: Construct a 5-event timeline (with dates) showing the transformation of a knight from a mounted warrior (c. 900) into a hereditary noble with judicial and fiscal privileges (c. 1200). Annotate each event with the structural change it represents.
questions.a: c. 900: Knight emerges as professional cavalryman (militarisation). c. 1000: Fief becomes hereditary (land = status). c. 1050: *Peace of God* movement limits private war (Church curbs violence). c. 1100: Primogeniture standardised (fief integrity). c. 1200: *Coutumes* grant seigneurial justice and taxation rights (public powers privatised). A poor timeline lists battles or kings instead of institutional shifts, showing the student confuses political narrative with social-structural evolution.
